questions.question: What is DNS and why does it exist?
questions.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's directory service that translates human-readable domain names like google.com into machine-readable IP addresses like 142.250.182.46. It exists because humans cannot memorize the numerical IP addresses of every website they visit — DNS bridges this gap, letting us use friendly names while machines still use IP addresses.

questions.question: Explain the DNS resolution hierarchy — which servers are involved and in what order?
questions.answer: The DNS resolution hierarchy has four layers: (1) Recursive Resolver — managed by the ISP, checks cache first; (2) Root DNS Servers — 13 sets globally, don't know IP addresses but know which TLD server to query; (3) TLD Nameservers — manage specific extensions like .com (VeriSign), .org (PIR), check if domain exists and redirect to authoritative server; (4) Authoritative Nameserver — the final answer, holds actual DNS records (A, CNAME, MX, etc.) and returns the IP address.

questions.question: What is Amazon Route 53?
questions.answer: Amazon Route 53 is AWS's highly available and scalable DNS web service. It provides three capabilities: domain registration (buying domain names), DNS routing (acting as an authoritative nameserver), and health checking (monitoring endpoints for automatic failover). The name comes from the famous US Route 66 highway and port 53, which is the standard DNS port.

questions.question: What is a hosted zone in Route 53?
questions.answer: A hosted zone is a container (DNS database) in Route 53 that stores all DNS records for a specific domain. When you create a hosted zone for a domain, Route 53 automatically assigns 4 authoritative nameservers to it. Hosted zones come in two types: public (accessible over the internet) and private (accessible only within specified AWS VPCs).

questions.question: What is TTL in DNS and why does it matter?
questions.answer: TTL (Time to Live) is the number of seconds a DNS record is cached by recursive resolvers before it must be refreshed from the authoritative nameserver. It matters because: (1) Higher TTL = fewer DNS queries, less load on your nameserver; (2) Lower TTL = faster propagation of DNS changes; (3) When planning DNS updates, you should lower TTL before the change and wait for the old TTL to expire so all caches refresh.

questions.question: Explain the difference between an A record, AAAA record, and CNAME record.
questions.answer: A record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address (e.g., saiguda.info → 54.23.11.45). AAAA record maps a domain name to an IPv6 address (4 times longer than IPv4 — hence 4 A's). CNAME (Canonical Name) maps one domain name to another domain name — an alias. For example, fb.com → facebook.com. Important restriction: CNAME cannot be used at the zone apex (root domain) — use Route 53 Alias records instead for AWS resources.

questions.question: What is an Alias record and how does it differ from a CNAME?
questions.answer: A Route 53 Alias record maps a domain name to an AWS resource endpoint (CloudFront, ALB, S3, API Gateway). Key differences from CNAME: (1) Alias records CAN be created at the zone apex (root domain like saiguda.info) — CNAMEs cannot; (2) Alias record queries are FREE — CNAMEs are charged per query; (3) Alias records automatically update when the underlying AWS resource's IP changes; (4) Alias records are a Route 53-specific feature, not standard DNS.

questions.question: What is OAC (Origin Access Control) in CloudFront?
questions.answer: OAC (Origin Access Control) is a CloudFront feature that allows a CloudFront distribution to securely access a private S3 bucket without making it public. When you enable OAC, CloudFront automatically updates the S3 bucket policy to allow only that specific CloudFront distribution to read from the bucket. This ensures users can only access website content through CloudFront (HTTPS, caching, CDN benefits) — not directly via an insecure S3 URL.

questions.question: Name the six Route 53 routing policies and briefly describe each.
questions.answer: (1) Simple — one record, one endpoint, no intelligence; (2) Weighted — split traffic by percentages, used for A/B testing; (3) Latency-based — routes to lowest-latency AWS region for the user; (4) Failover — routes to secondary when primary fails health check; (5) Geolocation — routes based on user's country/continent, not latency; (6) Multi-value — returns up to 8 healthy IPs, like DNS-level load balancing.

questions.question: What is the difference between a public and private hosted zone?
questions.answer: Public hosted zone: serves DNS queries from the internet, used for public-facing websites. Anyone globally can resolve domain names in it. Private hosted zone: only resolvable within specified AWS VPCs, used for internal services like microservices communicating via internal domain names (e.g., db.internal.myapp.com). Private zones are not accessible from the public internet.

questions.question: Your company bought a domain on GoDaddy but wants Route 53 for DNS. Walk me through the exact setup steps.
questions.answer: (Situation) Domain purchased on GoDaddy, DNS management needs to move to Route 53. (Task) Configure Route 53 as the authoritative nameserver. (Action) 1. Go to Route 53 → Create public hosted zone for the domain; 2. Route 53 generates 4 NS records; 3. Go to GoDaddy → My Domains → DNS → Name Servers → Change; 4. Replace GoDaddy's default nameservers with the 4 Route 53 NS values; 5. DNS propagation occurs — GoDaddy now forwards all DNS queries to Route 53. (Result) Within 24–48 hours, all DNS for the domain resolves through Route 53. Any records created in Route 53 hosted zone become the authoritative answers.

questions.question: You deployed a static website on S3 with a custom domain via Route 53 and CloudFront. Walk through the complete architecture and traffic flow.
questions.answer: (Situation) Static website needing global delivery, HTTPS, and a custom domain. (Task) Set up S3 + CloudFront + ACM + Route 53. (Action) 1. Create private S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled; 2. Create CloudFront distribution with S3 as origin, enable OAC (CloudFront updates S3 bucket policy automatically); 3. Request ACM certificate in us-east-1 for the domain, validate via DNS; 4. Attach ACM certificate to CloudFront, add custom domain; 5. Create Route 53 public hosted zone, add A Alias record pointing to CloudFront endpoint; 6. Update GoDaddy nameservers with Route 53 NS values. (Result) Traffic flow: User types saiguda.info → DNS resolves via Route 53 → Returns CloudFront endpoint → CloudFront serves from nearest edge location cache → Fetches from private S3 if not cached → HTTPS response to user.

questions.question: A DNS change you made 2 hours ago still hasn't propagated for some users. What are the likely causes and how do you diagnose?
questions.answer: (Situation) DNS change made, some users still see old record. (Task) Identify cause and resolve. (Action) 1. Check the record's TTL — if TTL was 3600s (1 hour) when changed, resolvers that cached right before the change will hold old record for up to 1 hour more; 2. Use dnschecker.org to check propagation status across global resolvers; 3. Try flushing your own machine's DNS cache (ipconfig /flushdns on Windows, sudo dscacheutil -flushcache on Mac); 4. Test directly against Route 53 nameservers using nslookup. (Result) Most likely cause is ISP resolver still has the old record cached per TTL. Best practice: lower TTL 24–48 hours before making DNS changes.

questions.question: Your application is deployed in two AWS regions. You want users to connect to the nearest region and automatically failover if one region goes down. How do you configure Route 53?
questions.answer: (Situation) Multi-region app needing low latency + automatic failover. (Task) Configure Route 53 routing for both goals. (Action) Use latency-based routing with health checks: 1. Create health checks for both regional endpoints; 2. Create two latency-based routing records — same domain, each pointing to a different region's endpoint; 3. Associate each record with its corresponding health check. (Result) Route 53 routes users to the lowest-latency region. If a region's health check fails, Route 53 stops returning that region's endpoint and all traffic goes to the healthy region automatically.

questions.question: You need to run an A/B test — 90% of users see the old app, 10% see the new version. How do you set this up in Route 53?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need A/B testing with precise traffic split. (Task) Configure Route 53 weighted routing. (Action) 1. Go to Route 53 hosted zone; 2. Create two A records with the same domain name — one pointing to old app server/endpoint (set weight to 90), one pointing to new app server/endpoint (set weight to 10); 3. Route 53 distributes traffic proportionally based on weights. (Result) 90% of DNS queries return the old server's IP, 10% return the new server's IP. When ready to fully switch, update weights to 0 and 100.

questions.question: A user's request for your website goes to the wrong S3 origin every time instead of the CloudFront edge cache. What might be wrong?
questions.answer: (Situation) CloudFront not serving from cache — always hitting S3 origin. (Task) Investigate caching behavior. (Action) Check: 1. CloudFront distribution default TTL and cache behaviors — maybe TTL is set to 0; 2. Check if S3 is returning Cache-Control: no-cache or no-store headers; 3. Verify the URL path matches a cache behavior in the distribution; 4. Check if query strings or headers are uncached and causing cache misses. (Result) Fix by ensuring appropriate Cache-Control headers on S3 objects and configuring CloudFront cache behavior with a reasonable TTL (e.g., 86400s for static files).

questions.question: What happens architecturally when you type a URL and press Enter? Cover DNS, TCP, and the AWS service chain.
questions.answer: (Situation) User types saiguda.info in browser. (Task) Trace the complete request journey. (Action) DNS phase: Browser checks local DNS cache → Queries recursive resolver (ISP) → Resolver checks cache → If miss: queries root DNS → root directs to .info TLD server → TLD directs to Route 53 authoritative servers → Route 53 returns CloudFront endpoint IP → IP cached per TTL. TCP phase: Browser opens TCP connection to CloudFront IP on port 443 (HTTPS). CloudFront phase: Checks edge location cache for requested object → If cache hit: returns immediately → If cache miss: fetches from S3 origin via OAC. S3 phase: Returns object to CloudFront → CloudFront caches it at edge → Sends to user. (Result) User sees website, subsequent requests are faster due to DNS and CDN caching.

questions.question: You need to serve different website versions to users in India vs. users in the EU for GDPR compliance. Which Route 53 routing policy and why?
questions.answer: (Situation) Content must differ by user's country for legal compliance. (Task) Route users to region-specific content. (Action) Use Geolocation routing: 1. Deploy India-specific version in ap-south-1, EU version in eu-west-1; 2. Create geolocation records in Route 53 — one for India pointing to ap-south-1 endpoint, one for EU pointing to eu-west-1 endpoint, one default for all other locations; 3. Route 53 inspects the source IP of DNS queries to determine geographic location. (Result) Indian users always reach the Indian version; EU users always reach the EU GDPR-compliant version. Note: This differs from latency-based routing which optimizes for speed, not compliance.

questions.question: Explain how call forwarding is an analogy for Route 53 nameserver updates.
questions.answer: When you buy a domain on GoDaddy but create your hosted zone in Route 53, the TLD server contacts GoDaddy (the registrar) when resolving your domain. GoDaddy checks its records and sees that the nameservers listed are Route 53's (not GoDaddy's own) — so it acts like call forwarding. GoDaddy says: 'I received this call, but I'm not the right person to answer — let me forward it to Route 53's nameservers.' The request is forwarded to Route 53's 4 nameservers, which hold the actual DNS records (hosted zone) and return the correct answer. This only works if you've updated GoDaddy's Name Server settings with Route 53's NS values.

questions.question: A startup deploys a website. Users can access it via the CloudFront URL but NOT via the custom domain. What are the most likely causes?
questions.answer: (Situation) CloudFront URL works, custom domain doesn't. (Task) Diagnose DNS misconfiguration. (Action) Check in order: 1. Has the Route 53 A Alias record been created for the custom domain pointing to the CloudFront endpoint? 2. Have the Route 53 nameservers been added to the domain registrar (GoDaddy)? Without this, DNS still resolves through GoDaddy's nameservers which have no records. 3. Has DNS propagated? Use dnschecker.org. 4. Has the custom domain (CNAME) been added to the CloudFront distribution's Alternate Domain Names? Without this, CloudFront rejects requests for the custom domain. 5. Is the ACM certificate attached to CloudFront? (Result) Most common causes are missing nameserver update in GoDaddy and custom domain not added to CloudFront distribution.

questions.question: Compare Route 53 Geolocation routing vs. Latency-based routing. When would you use each?
questions.answer: Latency-based routing: Routes users to the AWS region with the lowest network latency for their location. Best for performance-critical applications where speed matters most. A user in India might actually be routed to Singapore if Singapore has lower latency. Use when: you want the fastest possible experience, you have multiple regions deployed. Geolocation routing: Routes users based on their country or continent, regardless of latency. A user in India is routed to the India region even if Singapore would be faster. Use when: legal/compliance requirements (GDPR), content localization (language-specific sites), data residency laws, or geo-restricted content. Key difference: Latency = optimize for speed; Geolocation = optimize for location control.

questions.question: Design a highly available, globally distributed web application architecture using Route 53 and other AWS services. Justify each component.
questions.answer: Architecture: Route 53 (DNS + health checks + latency routing) → CloudFront (CDN, HTTPS termination, edge caching) → ALB in multiple regions (load distribution, SSL offloading) → Auto Scaling Groups with EC2 (compute, auto-scale) → RDS Multi-AZ (database, failover) → S3 (static assets, logs). Route 53 justification: Latency routing for performance, health checks for automatic failover, Alias records for cost-free DNS to ALBs. CloudFront: reduces origin load, improves latency globally, provides DDoS protection at edge. ALB: distributes traffic across AZs within a region, handles SSL. ASG: maintains capacity, scales with demand. RDS Multi-AZ: protects against AZ failure. Route 53 health checks monitor ALBs — if a region fails, traffic automatically routes to the next-lowest-latency region.

questions.question: What is the difference between Route 53 health checks and CloudWatch alarms? How can they work together?
questions.answer: Route 53 health checks: actively probe endpoints (HTTP/HTTPS/TCP) at regular intervals from multiple global locations. Primarily used to determine whether to include an endpoint in DNS responses (i.e., failover routing). CloudWatch alarms: monitor AWS metrics (CPU, request count, error rate, etc.) and trigger actions. They don't directly monitor external endpoints. Integration: You can create a Route 53 health check that monitors a CloudWatch alarm. If the alarm enters the ALARM state (e.g., high error rate on an ALB), the health check fails → Route 53 stops routing to that endpoint. This enables application-level failover (not just connectivity-level), making Route 53 aware of application health, not just server availability.

questions.question: Explain DNS propagation. Why can it take up to 48 hours, and what can you do to minimize propagation time?
questions.answer: DNS propagation is the time it takes for a DNS change to reach all recursive resolvers globally. It takes up to 48 hours because: (1) Every recursive resolver worldwide caches DNS records per TTL — a TTL of 48 hours means caches won't refresh for 2 days; (2) There are thousands of ISP resolvers globally, each with its own cache; (3) Some ISPs ignore TTL and cache for their own default duration. To minimize propagation time: (1) Lower your TTL to 60–300 seconds at least 24 hours BEFORE making the DNS change; (2) Wait for the old high TTL to expire (so all resolvers refresh with the new low TTL); (3) Make your DNS change — now it propagates within 60–300 seconds globally; (4) After confirming propagation, increase TTL again.

questions.question: A Route 53 hosted zone costs $0.50/month. You have 100 domains. How would you minimize Route 53 hosted zone costs?
questions.answer: Route 53 costs $0.50/month per hosted zone for the first 25, and $0.10/month for each additional zone. For 100 domains, you'd pay $25 × $0.50 + 75 × $0.10 = $12.50 + $7.50 = $20/month. Cost optimization strategies: (1) Consolidate subdomains — instead of separate hosted zones for app.company.com, api.company.com, admin.company.com, use one hosted zone for company.com with multiple records; (2) Use private hosted zones only when truly needed (internal services); (3) Delete hosted zones for unused/decommissioned domains immediately; (4) For simple static sites, consider using CloudFront with S3 and having the domain registrar handle DNS — avoiding a Route 53 hosted zone entirely if Route 53-specific routing features aren't needed. According to AWS documentation, the first 25 hosted zones are $0.50 each; additional zones are $0.10 each.
